lead: A reverse-biased p–n junction turns absorbed light into current: photons make electron–hole pairs, and the junction field sweeps the pairs out before they recombine. A plain PN diode collects only its thin depletion layer, so it is inefficient. Widening that layer into an intrinsic i region gives the PIN photodiode, the standard detector in fiber links from 0.85 µm to 1.55 µm. The collection mechanism, the efficiency–capacitance–speed trade-off, and the numbers a receiver designer uses follow.
prereq: You need Chapter 4.1 for η, R and photon energy; Unit 3 helps for absorption in direct-bandgap material.

sections.h3: Reverse bias turns photons into drift current

blocks.text: A PN photodiode is a p–n junction held in reverse bias. The reverse voltage widens the depletion region and strengthens its electric field. A photon with energy hν at least the bandgap E<sub>g</sub> is absorbed and creates an electron–hole pair. Inside the depletion region the field separates the pair at once: the electron drifts to the n side, the hole to the p side, and the movement is photocurrent. A pair created in the neutral p or n region has no strong field. It diffuses slowly and often recombines before reaching the junction, so it contributes little or nothing.

Efficiency follows from where absorption happens. A thin PN depletion gives small αw and low η. It also gives high junction capacitance C = εA/w, where ε = ε<sub>r</sub>ε<sub>0</sub>, A is area, and ε<sub>0</sub> = 8.85 × 10<sup>−12</sup> F/m. Thin w is fast but inefficient.

blocks.where: η is the fraction of incident photons that produce collected carriers; R is the facet reflectivity (fraction reflected); α is the absorption coefficient in m⁻¹; w is the depletion width in m. (1 − R) enters the semiconductor; (1 − e<sup>−αw</sup>) is absorbed in width w.

sections.h3: The PIN stack widens the collecting region

blocks.text: A PIN photodiode inserts an undoped i layer between p+ and n+ layers. Reverse bias depletes the i layer fully, so the field acts across the whole width. Light enters through a thin p+ layer because it must reach the i layer. An antireflection coating reduces R, often to a few percent. The i width can now be chosen for optics, not set by doping. Typical values are a few micrometres to about ten micrometres, giving large αw and η near 1 after allowing for reflection.

items: Silicon covers 0.85 µm, with responsivity around 0.5–0.6 A/W.
Germanium and InGaAs cover 1.3 µm and 1.55 µm.
InGaAs at 1.55 µm gives about 0.9 A/W.

blocks.text: A wide i layer lowers C, which helps the RC limit, but it raises transit time. The next section turns that trade-off into two bandwidth formulas.

sections.h3: Two bandwidth limits: transit time and RC

blocks.text: Carriers drift across the i layer at the saturation velocity v<sub>sat</sub>. The transit time is t = w/v<sub>sat</sub>. v<sub>sat</sub> is about 1 × 10⁵ m/s in Si and 6.5 × 10⁴ m/s in InGaAs. The junction capacitance C and load resistor R<sub>L</sub> form an RC limit. The smaller of the transit-time bandwidth and the RC bandwidth controls the diode.
t = w / v<sub>sat</sub>,   f<sub>t</sub> ≈ 0.4 / t,   C = εA / w,   f<sub>RC</sub> = 1 / (2πR<sub>L</sub>C)
blocks.where: t is transit time in s; w is i-layer width in m; v<sub>sat</sub> is saturation drift velocity in m/s; f<sub>t</sub> and f<sub>RC</sub> are bandwidths in Hz; C is capacitance in F; ε = ε<sub>r</sub>ε<sub>0</sub>; A is area in m²; R<sub>L</sub> is load resistance in Ω.

blocks.text: Design is a push–pull. Increasing w raises η and lowers C, so fRC improves; but t rises, so ft falls. Increasing A raises C and lowers fRC. A small area helps speed but makes fiber alignment harder. Reverse bias must be high enough to deplete the i layer and keep the field near saturation. For a high-speed receiver, choose w so ft and fRC are both above the bit rate, then accept the resulting η. Avalanche gain can raise sensitivity later (see Chapter 4.3).

figure.caption: Light passes through the antireflection coating and thin p+ layer; the fully depleted i layer sweeps photon-made pairs to the contacts as photocurrent, which flows through the load resistor.

spec.title: Front-illuminated PIN photodiode
spec.aria: Vertical stack from incoming light through antireflection coating, thin p+ layer, wide undoped i layer where pairs are swept, n+ layer, and the load resistor that receives the photocurrent.

examples.question: An InGaAs PIN photodiode for 1.55 µm has i-layer width w = 4 µm, absorption coefficient α = 1 × 10⁴ cm⁻¹, facet reflectivity R = 0.03, area A = 1 × 10⁻⁸ m², relative permittivity ε<sub>r</sub> = 13.9, and load resistance R<sub>L</sub> = 50 Ω. The saturation drift velocity is 6.5 × 10⁴ m/s. Find η, the transit time, the transit-time bandwidth, the junction capacitance, and the RC bandwidth. Which limit controls?
steps: Convert w to cm for the αw product: w = 4 µm = 4 × 10⁻⁴ cm. Then αw = (1 × 10⁴ cm⁻¹)(4 × 10⁻⁴ cm) = 4.0, dimensionless.
Absorbed fraction in the i layer = 1 − e<sup>−4</sup> = 1 − 0.0183 = 0.9817.
Transit time t = w/v<sub>sat</sub> = (4 × 10⁻⁶ m)/(6.5 × 10⁴ m/s) = 6.154 × 10⁻¹¹ s = 61.54 ps.
Transit-time bandwidth f<sub>t</sub> ≈ 0.4/t = 0.4/(6.154 × 10⁻¹¹ s) = 6.50 × 10⁹ Hz = 6.50 GHz.
Capacitance C = ε<sub>r</sub>ε<sub>0</sub>A/w = (13.9 × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m × 1 × 10⁻⁸ m²)/(4 × 10⁻⁶ m) = 3.075 × 10⁻¹³ F ≈ 0.308 pF.
RC bandwidth f<sub>RC</sub> = 1/(2πR<sub>L</sub>C) = 1/(2π × 50 Ω × 3.075 × 10⁻¹³ F) = 1.035 × 10¹⁰ Hz = 10.35 GHz.
The smaller bandwidth is f<sub>t</sub> = 6.50 GHz, so transit time limits this diode.
examples.answer: η = 0.952, t = 61.54 ps, f<sub>t</sub> = 6.50 GHz, C = 0.308 pF, f<sub>RC</sub> = 10.35 GHz; the diode is transit-time limited.
examples.check:
import math
alpha=1e4
w_cm=4e-4
R=0.03
eta=(1-R)*(1-math.exp(-alpha*w_cm))
w=4e-6
vsat=6.5e4
t=w/vsat
f_t=0.4/t
A=1e-8
eps_r=13.9
eps0=8.85e-12
RL=50.0
C=eps_r*eps0*A/w
f_RC=1/(2*math.pi*RL*C)
print(round(eta,3))
print(round(t*1e12,2))
print(round(f_t/1e9,1))
print(round(C*1e12,3))
print(round(f_RC/1e9,2))

traps: A thicker i layer is not automatically better: it raises η but increases transit time and lowers f<sub>t</sub>.
Do not drop (1 − R). A 3% reflection loses 3% of the incident power before absorption.
Convert units before using αw: α in m⁻¹ with w in m, or α in cm⁻¹ with w in cm. Mixing cm and m gives a wrong exponent.
The RC limit is 1/(2πR<sub>L</sub>C), not 0.4/t. Check both and take the smaller.
A photodiode works in reverse bias; forward bias injects current and destroys photodetection.

quiz.q: What does the i in PIN stand for, and what does that layer do?
quiz.a: It stands for intrinsic. The wide undoped i layer is fully depleted in reverse bias, so its field sweeps photon-made electron–hole pairs out as photocurrent.

quiz.q: Why do pairs made in the neutral p and n regions contribute little photocurrent?
quiz.a: They are outside the strong junction field. They move mainly by slow diffusion and many recombine before reaching the depletion region.

quiz.q: A Si PIN photodiode has facet reflectivity R = 0.05 and αw = 2.0. Find its quantum efficiency.
A designer doubles the i-layer width w and keeps area and material unchanged. State the effect on η, C, t, f<sub>t</sub> and f<sub>RC</sub>.
quiz.a: η rises because αw is larger. C falls roughly by half because C = εA/w. t doubles because t = w/v<sub>sat</sub>. f<sub>t</sub> falls by about half because f<sub>t</sub> ≈ 0.4/t. f<sub>RC</sub> rises by about a factor of two because C is halved. Transit time becomes more likely to control.

quiz.q: Which detector material is usual at 1.55 µm, and what responsivity is typical?
quiz.a: InGaAs is usual at 1.55 µm, with responsivity about 0.9 A/W.

quiz.q: Why is the p+ layer thin in a front-illuminated PIN photodiode?
quiz.a: Light enters through the p+ side, so a thin p+ layer reduces absorption and loss before the light reaches the wide i layer where collection happens.

quiz.q: An InGaAs PIN has w = 5 µm and v<sub>sat</sub> = 6.5 × 10⁴ m/s. Find the transit time and transit-time bandwidth.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production receivers use waveguide photodiodes and back-illuminated structures to shrink transit distance without shrinking absorption. Germanium-on-silicon photodiodes bring 1.55 µm detection into CMOS photonics. Balanced photodiodes and coherent receivers handle phase and polarization. Search next for waveguide photodiode, back-illuminated PIN, and Ge-on-Si photodetector.
